title: The Mongol Decimal Army
text:
When Temujin was proclaimed Chinggis Khan in 1206, he united steppe peoples who had spent generations raiding and betraying each other. To hold them together, he reorganized his whole people on a decimal system.

Men were grouped in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and, at the largest scale, ten thousand, each with its own commander. According to the Secret History of the Mongols, Chinggis named the commanders of ninety-five units of a thousand, rewarding loyal companions rather than old tribal chiefs. Crucially, many units were deliberately formed by mixing men from different clans and tribes, including defeated enemies. Loyalty shifted from the tribe to the unit and to the khan.

The units lived, traveled and fought together, and their members were bound to one another. The Franciscan friar John of Plano Carpini, who visited the Mongols in the 1240s, reported harsh rules of collective responsibility: if one or two men of a group of ten fled in battle, all ten were put to death, and if a man was captured and his comrades did not try to free him, they too were punished.

Promotion was based on ability and loyalty. Chinggis also created an elite guard drawn from the sons of commanders, which served as both a training school and a check on the units. With this structure, a people of perhaps a million built the largest contiguous land empire in history.
lesson: Small units with shared responsibility create strong bonds. Organizing people around the team rather than old loyalties can unify a divided group.
people: Chinggis Khan (Genghis Khan), John of Plano Carpini
source: The Secret History of the Mongols (13th century); John of Plano Carpini, History of the Mongols (c. 1247)
caveat: Population estimates for the early Mongol nation are rough; Carpini's account of collective punishment is an outsider's report.
